newsitem.title: GERMANY: Are German-made cars becoming a thing of the past?.
newsitem.headline: Are German-made cars becoming a thing of the past?.

text.p: When is a German car really a German car? Not as often as you might think.

German carmakers, making good on promises for international expansion, produced 12 percent more cars in foreign plants last year while domestic output rose a mere four percent, the VDA German automobile association said on Wednesday.
More important, about one in 10 cars -- or about 235,000 -- sold last year under German brands were actually made abroad but then imported to Germany and put up for sale, the VDA said.

"Production by German manufacturers in foreign countries clearly rose last year and the globalisation will become increasingly clear in the coming years," VDA President Bernd Gottschalk told the association's annual news conference.

The report in general said the car industry faces a delicate year in 1997 with production likely to grow at two to three percent compared with four percent in 1996 but remain heavily dependent on exports.

The VDA report also confirmed the growing trend of foreign expansion by carmakers seeking to tap into emerging markets, notably in Asia and Latin America, where hungry car buyers and also cheap labour can be quickly found in the same place.

Leaders in the foreign output surge were Volkswagen AG's VW brand and its Audi luxury car unit, with VW's foreign production rising seven percent to 2.08 million units and Audi's output surging to 21,120 units from 1,152 in 1995.
BMW, which makes the highly-successful Z3 roadster at a U.S. factory in South Carolina, more than doubled its foreign production to 69,313 units last year, the VDA said.

VW was also a leader in selling imported cars under the VW name, with 59,762 such vehicles sold last year in Germany. Only Ford Motor Co's German unit, Ford-Werke AG, topped VW with imports of 160,461 units from European production sites.

The report also said German carmakers produced some 2.788 million vehicles abroad last year, up from 2.492 million a year earlier, while production in Germany rose to only 4.843 million vehicle compared with 4.667 million units in 1995.

Exports were the engine behind the growth as the number of vehicles produced in Germany but earmarked for foreign markets rose 7.5 percent to 2.65 million vehicles and accounted for 58 percent of overall domestic production.
But the VDA said its data showed only three percent growth to 2.117 million vehicles in the number of German-made cars that were actually sold in Germany.
"That shows the increasing degree of international complexity facing vehicle production," Gottschalk said.
Foreign production is also being matched with investment.

Gottschalk, the former chief of Mercedes-Benz's truck division, said direct foreign investments last year totalled about 4.5 billion marks ($2.7 billion), which was worth about 40 percent of the total automobile industry investments made in Germany.
But he said foreign investment helped secure jobs in Germany at a time of nagging high unemployment, saying three jobs abroad generally creates or maintain a job in Germany.

German car industry companies reduced the total size of their domestic workforce by 0.6 percent last year to 657,100 employees. But the figure is sharply below the peak in 1991 of more than 760,000 workers.

Gottschalk also said a top priority for the German car industry was to reduce costs and taxes to boost domestic investment since German car industry hourly wages last year were on average 62 marks -- nearly double France at 33 marks and Britain's 27 marks.
